analysis.one_liner: Phases out federal subsidies, tax breaks, and liability shields for oil, gas, and coal companies.
analysis.headline: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and 32 Democratic cosponsors but never received a hearing or vote, dying in committee when the term ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strip away a long list of federal advantages enjoyed by fossil fuel companies: dozens of tax breaks, higher royalties for drilling and mining on public land, removal of caps on what companies owe after offshore and pipeline spills, and a ban on federal agencies and export-credit agencies financing fossil fuel projects abroad. It would also repeal special permitting that Congress gave the Mountain Valley Pipeline and raise taxes on coal to fund black lung benefits for miners. It was introduced in May 2024, sent to nine House committees, and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, taxpayers would have gained revenue now forgone through industry-specific tax deductions, credits, and accounting rules; communities near offshore rigs and pipelines would have gained stronger liability if a spill happened; coal miners' black lung fund would have gained a larger excise tax; and renewable energy producers would have competed on a more level playing field. The Treasury would also have had to identify and report remaining subsidies not covered by the bill.

how_it_helps.text: Terminates dozens of fossil-fuel-specific tax preferences, including the enhanced oil recovery credit, percentage depletion for oil, gas, and coal, immediate expensing of intangible drilling costs, last-in-first-out inventory accounting for oil, gas, and coal companies, the corporate tax exemption for fossil-fuel publicly traded partnerships, and fossil-fuel carve-outs from bonus depreciation, the research credit, and foreign-derived income rules.

Raises federal royalty rates for coal, oil, and gas produced on public lands from 12.5% (or 16.67%) to 18.75% and bans future royalty relief on offshore leases, so the public collects more for resources taken from federal land.

Removes liability caps for offshore facilities and for onshore pipelines carrying tar sands oil, and denies tax deductions for oil spill removal costs and damages, shifting spill costs back onto the companies responsible.

Bars the Export-Import Bank, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, USAID, the Millennium Challenge Corporation, and U.S. contributions to international financial institutions from financing fossil fuel projects, and terminates the Department of Energy's Office of Fossil Energy and its fossil fuel loan and research programs.

Repeals the Fiscal Responsibility Act provisions that fast-tracked the Mountain Valley Pipeline and rewrote environmental review, and repeals Inflation Reduction Act provisions requiring offshore oil and gas lease sales.

Raises the excise tax that funds the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund from $1.10 to $1.38 per ton, and the oil spill liability trust fund tax from 9 to 10 cents per barrel, and adds a 13% severance tax on crude oil and natural gas taken from the Gulf of Mexico outer continental shelf.
Requires the Treasury Department to compile a report of every remaining federal subsidy for fossil fuel production and to eliminate those it finds in the tax depreciation system.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal companies would pay through higher taxes, loss of deductions and credits, higher royalties on public land, unlimited spill liability for offshore and tar sands pipeline operations, and exposure of their large lenders to cleanup costs. Some portion of the new excise and severance taxes could be passed through to consumers in fuel prices. Also affected: banks and asset managers above $10 billion (banks) or $250 billion (investment firms), which would lose immunity from cleanup liability under the Superfund law, and the carbon capture and refining coal industries, which would lose federal credits.

drawbacks.text: The bill layers on new taxes on production — a 13% severance tax on Gulf of Mexico crude and natural gas, a 10-cents-per-barrel spill fund tax, and higher black lung coal taxes — which producers can pass through to consumers at the pump and in utility bills.

It repeals tax breaks and programs abruptly for costs incurred after enactment, which would raise operating costs for coal-reliant regions and fossil fuel workers whose communities depend on the industry; the bill contains no transition assistance for those workers.

It terminates the 45Q carbon capture credit entirely and blocks Department of Energy funds for carbon capture projects, going further than many climate advocates would: some support keeping capture incentives for heavy industry and existing plants rather than ending them.
Repealing the Fiscal Responsibility Act's permitting reforms would restore slower, longer environmental reviews for energy infrastructure generally, not only fossil fuel projects.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the upside is concrete: billions in industry-specific tax breaks ended, higher royalties on public resources, real spill liability, and a bigger black lung fund. The honest costs are that some of the new taxes would reach consumers through fuel prices and that coal and oil-field communities get nothing in the bill to cushion the hit. A narrower version with a longer phase-in and worker transition aid would have been easier to defend, but the core subsidy removal is soundly aimed at shifting costs from taxpayers and pollution victims back onto producers.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to nine House committees and then to subcommittees, and no committee ever held a hearing or markup, so it died when the term ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced the End Polluter Welfare Act of 2024 on May 23, 2024, with 32 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.

The Speaker referred it to nine committees at once — Ways and Means plus Natural Resources, Transportation, Financial Services, Science, Agriculture, Energy and Commerce, Foreign Affairs, and Appropriations — a structure that splits a bill among many committees with their own agendas.

Over the next seven months it was sent down to three subcommittees: Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials in May, Commodity Markets, Digital Assets, and Rural Development in October, and Trade in December.
No committee reported the bill, no hearing or markup is recorded, and no floor vote ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal producers came out ahead: by never reaching a vote, the bill left in place every tax break, royalty rate, liability cap, and federal financing channel it would have eliminated.

for.name: Rep. Ilhan Omar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 32 original cosponsors.

for.name: 32 Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors, incl. Jayapal, Khanna, Pressley, Tlaib, Raskin, Schiff
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors on introduction day; no Republican joined.

for.name: Environmental and government-waste watchdog groups
for.role: Outside supporters of ending fossil fuel subsidies
for.what_they_did: Promoted the End Polluter Welfare Act concept publicly as a way to recover taxpayer money and curb pollution.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of primary jurisdiction
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup of the bill in the seven months after referral, the step needed before any tax bill can reach the floor.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Controlled the chamber's agenda and the nine referred committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill in any of the committees that received it; no committee reported it out.

against.name: Fossil fuel industry
against.role: Companies, trade groups, and their lobbying operations
against.what_they_did: Maintained long-running lobbying campaigns to preserve the tax preferences, royalty rates, and liability limits the bill targeted.

sides.party_line_note: All 32 cosponsors were Democrats from the party's progressive wing and no Republican sponsored or supported the bill, while the Republican House majority that controlled the committees never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill ends most of their federal tax advantages (percentage depletion, expensed drilling costs, LIFO accounting, MLP tax exemption, credits), raises public-land royalties to 18.75%, adds a 13% Gulf severance tax, and removes their offshore and tar sands pipeline liability caps. Consumers ultimately share some of the cost through fuel prices, which is why the industry's stake runs against the public's here.

Coal loses percentage depletion, capital-gains treatment for royalties, refined coal credits, and clean coal project credits, while its black lung excise tax rises from $1.10 to $1.38 per ton and royalties on federal leases rise to 18.75%. The bill gives nothing to coal-dependent communities, whose job losses the public would otherwise bear.

industries.industry: Pipelines and midstream (incl. Mountain Valley Pipeline)
industries.note: The bill repeals the law that fast-tracked the Mountain Valley Pipeline, slows depreciation for natural gas gathering lines, and extends full spill liability to pipelines carrying tar sands oil. These provisions matter because pipeline spills impose cleanup and health costs on nearby communities today.

Banks with $10 billion or more in assets and investment firms with $250 billion or more lose their immunity from Superfund cleanup liability as lenders to polluting sites, meaning taxpayers and communities are less likely to be left holding cleanup costs when a polluter goes bankrupt.

industries.industry: Carbon capture and clean energy technology firms
industries.note: The bill terminates the 45Q carbon sequestration credit, ends DOE carbon capture funding, and eliminates refined coal's renewable electricity credit, though it narrows rather than ends the clean hydrogen credit. This is the one place the bill cuts support for technologies some climate advocates want to keep.
